title: DeepSeek v4.1 Flash Powers Reverse Engineering Workflow
summary: Engineer cuts reverse engineering timelines from years to months using DeepSeek v4.1 Flash with Ghidra, hypothesis-driven debugging, and structured Markdown
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- A reverse engineer reports DeepSeek v4.1 Flash cuts project timelines from years to six months on hardware and software reverse engineering tasks.
- The workflow pairs Ghidra decompilation with structured Markdown notes and hypothesis-driven debugging loops to prevent AI agents from getting stuck.
- Real projects include typewriters, cameras, synthesizers, and e-readers, with custom agent skills forcing testable experiments instead of random guessing.


A veteran hardware and software reverse engineer has published a detailed field report showing how DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, paired with Ghidra and a disciplined agent-skill architecture, compresses multi-year reverse engineering projects into six-month timelines. The workflow, shared on Hacker News in November 2026, centers on forcing AI agents to maintain structured Markdown documentation and test hypotheses systematically rather than guess randomly.


## Workflow Architecture and Agent Skills


The engineer's process begins by pointing DeepSeek v4.1 Flash at a target binary and invoking a set of custom agent skills stored in a local .agents directory. The core innovation is not the AI itself but the disciplined framework: agents must document every discovery in Markdown files, maintaining a clear audit trail that prevents the circular reasoning common in autonomous debugging sessions.


Three critical skills anchor the workflow. First, a Ghidra bridge skill (publicly shared as ghidra-decompile-skill) provides 22 targeted decompilation scripts and fixes version mismatches between the GhidraMCP extension and Ghidra releases. Second, a hypothesis-debugging skill forces agents into a scientific method loop: state one testable hypothesis, design a definitive experiment, log results in CSV format, then iterate. Third, tooling-specific skills describe how to use radare2, Kuna, or the MCP Ghidra bridge, preventing agents from abandoning tasks when they hit tool-specific friction.


## Real-World Project Results


The engineer reports completing reverse engineering projects on typewriters, cameras, synthesizers, and e-readers in the past six months, each of which would have required years of manual assembly analysis. One example involved deciphering a proprietary save file format for a paid application, then pivoting to clean software development to build a custom editor. The workflow blurs the line between reverse engineering and greenfield development, with the engineer noting they built a custom Photoshop alternative (distinct from ArtCraft suite) about a year before similar tools emerged publicly.


The acceleration comes not from replacing human expertise but augmenting it. Twenty years of assembly and hardware knowledge guide the agent toward correct approaches, while the AI handles tedious instruction-by-instruction analysis. The engineer emphasizes that curiosity remains the driver, with LLMs serving as a turbo boost rather than a replacement for understanding.


## Hypothesis-Driven Debugging as Control Mechanism


The hypothesis-debugging skill represents a critical control mechanism for preventing agent hallucination and endless loops. When an agent gets stuck, the skill enforces a strict sequence: document the current state in Markdown, formulate one falsifiable hypothesis about why the code behaves as observed, design an experiment that will definitively confirm or reject the hypothesis, execute the experiment, log the outcome in a CSV file, and repeat. This discipline, borrowed from the scientific method, eliminates the random trial-and-error that derails many AI-assisted debugging sessions.


The workflow also addresses a common failure mode where agents give up too quickly when faced with unfamiliar tooling. By encoding reverse engineering tool usage into dedicated skills (how to invoke radare2 commands, how to query Ghidra's decompiler API), the system ensures agents have concrete next steps even when encountering obscure binary formats or non-standard instruction sets.


## Release Date and Availability


Officially released on November 19, 2026, the field report and associated agent skills are publicly available through GitHub repositories. The ghidra-decompile-skill and hypothesis-debugging repositories allow other reverse engineers to replicate the workflow immediately. The engineer uses DeepSeek v4.1 Flash as the primary model, citing its combination of speed and reasoning capability for disassembly analysis.


## What This Means


This field report offers concrete evidence that LLMs paired with disciplined workflows can dramatically accelerate specialized technical work without replacing domain expertise. The key insight is structural: the value comes not from raw model capability but from agent skills that enforce documentation, hypothesis testing, and tool-specific knowledge. For reverse engineers, hardware hackers, and security researchers, the workflow provides a template for compressing timelines while maintaining the curiosity and understanding that drive exploratory work. The public release of the skills lowers the barrier for others to adopt similar practices in 2026 and beyond.
